data.title: Former Air Force secretary questions 'advice' Trump received before starting Iran war
data.description:
Former Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall III on Sunday questioned the “advice” President Trump received in the lead-up to the Iran war.

“What I don’t understand, frankly, about the Iran war is what advice was given to the president that led him to start this conflict?” Kendall told host Martha Raddatz on ABC’s “This Week.”

The Iran conflict has entered its seventh month, with the U.S. and Islamic Republic exchanging strikes this weekend and no sign of a deal to end hostilities. The war has resulted in the deaths of 18 U.S. service members and thousands of Iranian civilians. 

The conflict has also burned up many of the American military’s missile interceptors, and the Pentagon has reached deals in recent weeks with multiple defense contractors to boost production. 

While the initial joint U.S.-Israeli operation in February resulted in the death of Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, his son, Mojtaba Khamenei, has succeeded him as supreme leader and Iranian officials are still expressing hardline views toward the U.S.

Noting Trump did not receive authorization from Congress to launch the war, Kendall said “the results of the initial strike have been about as one would have” predicted.

“The illusion that the Iranian regime would suddenly fall and this would be a very short conflict was not one that’s been held by anybody else until now,” added Kendall, who led the Air Force during the Biden administration.

The president on Friday equated the war to “small potatoes” and said he “can understand” why Vice President Vance claims he does not view the conflict as a war.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright, though, acknowledged Sunday the U.S. is “still in a conflict” with Iran. 

“It’s a challenge,” he told Raddatz earlier on “This Week.” “Iran is doing everything they can to cling on to something.”

The war also sparked higher gas prices in the U.S., as the Iranian military has restricted traffic through the crucial Strait of Hormuz. Gas prices are the highest they have ever been on Labor Day weekend, as roughly $4.14 per gallon, according to AAA.

data.title: Energy secretary: 'I don't want to have an opinion' on rising gas prices
data.description:
Energy Secretary Chris Wright on Sunday said he did not “want to have an opinion” on the direction of gas prices Americans are paying, which are above $4 per gallon on average at the pump in the U.S.

“You said on this show five months ago that high gas prices had peaked, but between not just the Iran war, but the Russia-Ukraine war and the U.S.’s own dwindling reserves, isn’t it possible gas prices could go up even more?” CNN’s Dana Bash asked Wright on “State of the Union.”

“Look, I don’t want to have an opinion on that, but if you look at the futures market right now, what can you buy gasoline for two months in advance from where we are today? It’s down more than 30 cents a gallon from where it is today,” Wright responded.

Bash pressed Wright further on the direction of gas prices, to which he responded that, “if I had to guess, they’re more likely to go down than go up.”

According to AAA, the average cost of a gallon of regular gas in the U.S. was about $4.15 on Sunday morning, up from about $3.20 last year at this time.

The Iran war, which recently hit the six-month mark, has driven up oil and gas prices as the Strait of Hormuz has been closed amid the conflict. The high gas prices have come alongside wider concerns about the American economy, spelling trouble for the president and his party as November’s midterms near.

President Trump has faced pressure over the war, tied to the conflict’s impact on affordability and its reported effects on the U.S. military’s munitions stockpiles.

On Wednesday, the president downplayed the war’s impact on Republican candidates.

“I don’t think it will be very much longer,” Trump said when asked about other Iranian targets the U.S. can hit.

“And I’m not affected by the election. Number one, I’m not running, but my party’s running, and I’m going to help my party. But I think my party respects the fact that we’re not allowing Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”

data.title: The Faster Labor Contracts Act would give workers a fair shot at a better life
data.description:
Labor Day reminds me of a moment in my childhood. I couldn’t have been more than five years old, sitting on my grandfather’s knee and listening to stories about his journey from Ireland through Ellis Island. He taught me more than family history. He taught me what hard work could make possible  — and how his membership in the Iron Workers union gave him the security and opportunity to build the better life he had crossed an ocean in search of.

For too many families today, that dream has slipped out of reach. The Faster Labor Contracts Act is one way I am working to restore it — by giving workers a fairer path to the security, opportunity and upward mobility that helped change the course of my own family.

The pressures facing working families are not abstract. Housing, health care, education, childcare and everyday necessities consume more of the family budget. Wages have struggled to keep pace. And even workers who exercise their legal right to organize can spend months — or years — waiting for their first contract that actually moves them forward.

A new Gallup report shows labor unions with a 71 percent approval rating, the highest in recent history, with support extending across Independents, Republicans and Democrats. It’s easy to understand why. Research shows that union workers earn over 11 percent more than their nonunion peers and are more likely to have employer-sponsored health coverage and access to paid sick leave.

Yet only 10 percent of Americans belong to unions today.

When workers seek to organize, they can face sophisticated anti-union campaigns, designed to discourage them from exercising that right. Where these tactics fail, some employers refuse to bargain in good faith altogether. As a result, it takes almost a year and a half on average for workers to negotiate a first contract.

The consequences extend well beyond the bargaining table. The decline in union membership has coincided with the eroding standard of living for middle-class families. As bargaining power for workers has decreased, we’ve seen income inequality skyrocket, wages stagnate, and less economic mobility than ever before.

This is not the American Dream that brought my family away from the emerald shores of Ireland, and it’s not the American Dream working families yearn for as they agonize over how to afford a home, educate their children, pay their medical bills, or simply keep pace with the rising cost of everyday life.

The Faster Labor Contracts Act would address one of the clearest failures in the current system. It would require employers to begin bargaining within 10 days of notification from a new union. If an agreement isn’t reached after 90 days of good-faith negotiations, the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service would step in unless both parties agree to extend negotiations. If mediation still fails to produce an agreement, federal arbitrators could then issue a binding two-year decision to resolve the impasse.

I have seen the importance of that principle firsthand in my own community, Pennsylvania’s 1st District. When our nurses at St. Mary Medical Center in Bucks County voted to organize, I supported their decision and their right to have a meaningful voice in the workplace.

The same standard should apply wherever Pennsylvania workers choose to organize. At UPMC Magee-Women’s Hospital in Pittsburgh, nearly 1,000 nurses and advanced practitioners voted last year to form a union and strengthen their voice for their patients and profession. In first-contract negotiations, they have sought stronger staffing standards, compensation that helps retain experienced nurses, and expanded benefits, including parental leave. More than a year later, they remain without an agreement.

That is where the Faster Labor Contracts Act matters. A vote to organize should begin a meaningful bargaining process, not an indefinite waiting game. When workers have made their choice and come to the table in good faith, delay should not be allowed to render that choice meaningless.

That same commitment to protecting the economic security of working families is also driving my work with SEIU on the Good Jobs for Good Airports Act. Across the Philadelphia region, airport service workers can lose hard-earned wages and benefits simply because a new contractor takes over. A change in contractor should not mean a step backward for the people doing the work. In both cases, the principle is simple: Hard work should still provide a fair path to stability, opportunity and a better future.

Working Americans are facing a rising cost of living, wages that have struggled to keep pace, and an economy in which too many families feel they are working harder simply to tread water. We need the Faster Labor Contracts Act to restore balance, strengthen workers’ bargaining power, and ensure that choosing to organize leads to a fair and timely first contract.

This Labor Day, the Senate has an opportunity to renew a basic American promise: that hard work should still lead to a better life. I call on my colleagues to pass the FLCA, stand on the side of American workers, and help ensure that promise remains within reach for the next generation.

Brian Fitzpatrick represents Pennsylvania’s 1st Congressional District in the U.S. House of Representatives.

data.title: Former Air Force secretary says he 'couldn't serve' in Trump administration
data.description:
Former Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall III said Sunday he “couldn’t serve” in the Trump administration, blasting Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s leadership of the Pentagon.

“I’ve never seen an attempt to politicize our military like the one being conducted by Pete Hegseth,” Kendall told Martha Raddatz on ABC’s “This Week.”

Earlier this week, Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned after months of strife with Hegseth. Hegseth also ousted Army chief of staff Gen. Randy George in April and has blocked promotions of four Army officers with ties to branch officials he fired.

The Defense secretary also removed six Army officers from two-star general consideration earlier this week, a source familiar with the matter told The Hill.

Kendall, who led the Air Force during the Biden administration, said Hegseth imposing his will on the armed services “is rippling all the way down through the ranks” of the military.

“It’s causing people to be afraid and … in many cases I think he’s not getting good advice. Because people are afraid to tell him things that he doesn’t want to hear,” he told Raddatz, referring to Hegseth.

“Very good people that I know are leaving because of the climate of fear and because of the things the military is being asked to do,” Kendall added.

Given that “climate of fear” Kendall referenced, the former Air Force secretary said senior military officers have an “obligation” to “stand up” to administration officials attempting to “do something which is morally wrong, unethical” or illegal.

“I’m afraid they’re not doing that,” Kendall said, later pointing out the ongoing U.S. military campaign on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific Ocean — which he called “unconstitutional.”

Later in the interview, Raddatz asked Kendall what he would do if he were still Air Force secretary. But he dismissed the premise of her question, saying, “I couldn’t serve in this administration.”

data.title: Wright: US 'may not' reach nuclear agreement with Iran
data.description:
Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Sunday the Trump administration “may not” reach a nuclear agreement with the Iranian regime.

“There may not be a nuclear agreement. It may be simply destroying their capabilities to do it,” Wright told host Martha Raddatz on ABC’s “This Week.”

The Energy secretary added a nuclear agreement with the Islamic Republic “may await a next administration.”

The Middle Eastern conflict has entered its seventh month, with no sign of a deal between the U.S. and Iran to end military hostilities and curb the latter’s nuclear program. The U.S. and Israel launched the war in late February, with President Trump and administration officials saying the goal was to destroy Iran’s nuclear capabilities. 

American forces on Saturday fired on multiple Iranian crude oil carriers in response to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) attacking two U.S. warships, U.S. Central Command said.

IRGC forces retaliated on Sunday by striking an American ship in the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian state media reported. 

Trump on Friday called the conflict “small potatoes” for the U.S. and said he “can understand” Vice President Vance saying he does not view the conflict in Iran as a war.

“I call it a military conflict because it’s small potatoes for us. It’s not a big thing,” Trump said of the war, which has resulted in the deaths of 18 U.S. service members and thousands of Iranian civilians. 

Wright said Sunday the U.S. has to “destroy” Iran’s nuclear capabilities, saying American forces are “degrading their capacity to develop nuclear weapons and, ultimately, to deliver them if they develop one.”

He told Raddatz, “This is not trivial, but the United States will get the job done. And we will work in cooperation with our allies in the region.”

data.title: Jared Isaacman's support for Musk's space data centers did not occur in a vacuum
data.description:
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman’s support for Elon Musk’s idea to put AI data centers in space and power them with solar panels did not occur in a vacuum. It comes not just against a background of rising, bipartisan opposition to ground-based data centers but also the recent announcement of an immense, SpaceX Starbase to be built in Louisiana.

Many people oppose data centers out of the same kind of “NIMBY” emotion that fueled opposition to nuclear power plants and hydraulic fracking. They view them as big, noisy eyesores that will consume a lot of electricity and water to the detriment of local communities.

Opposition to ground-based AI data centers is not universal. Trade unions, which foresee lots of jobs being created in their construction and operation, are warmly supporting them. On the other hand, if Meta’s experiments with using robots at data centers pans out, those jobs may be fewer than many expect.

The reason that many people are opposed to AI data centers in their communities may have less to do with objective facts than a Chinese disinformation campaign to turn them against such facilities. Engadget reports that X uncovered a Chinese bot farm with 200,000 accounts, 200 of which were used to manipulate the debate about data centers.

It should be noted that the Chinese are going pedal to the metal to create their own data centers. As a totalitarian country, China is not concerned with public opinion one way or the other. Beijing is determined to dominate AI according to its ideology and interests.

Musk thinks he has an answer to the nimby problem on AI data centers by deploying them in space. In the latter stages, at least, the data centers would be manufactured on the moon and launched from the lunar surface.

The recent announcement of a launch facility called Star Base Louisiana is likely part of that vision. SpaceX plans to build 10 launch pads on the Louisiana coast capable of launching and recovering 1,000 Starships per year. Thatis more than enough to facilitate the lunar base, the orbital data center constellation, and eventually the Mars settlement that are the basis of Musk’s vision for the future.

A coalition of environmental groups is already raising objections to Star Base Louisiana. The Louisiana Wildlife Federation, National Wildlife Federation and Pontchartrain Conservancy have complained that the proposed regulations would waive 13 different wildlife, water and public health laws for space development projects.

Currently, it is unknown how the objections will hamper the construction and operation of the $100 billion facility. Environmentalists have hampered Star Base Boca Chica to a certain extent. Expect a similar effort directed toward the Louisiana facility.

Even if all or most of the AI data centers are deployed in space, as Musk envisions and Isaacman supports, the disquiet that many people feel toward AI will not be entirely soothed. The fear that AI will destroy jobs or, as a lot of science fiction has envisioned, destroy the human species is widespread. Many people have seen the Terminator movies, which envision an AI system called Skynet going rogue and waging war on humanity.

Fear of AI is likely overblown. While the technology will make some jobs obsolete, it will also create even more jobs. The future will belong to people who have the knowledge to interact with AI systems and guide them for the benefit of humankind. Obviously, humans must always be in the loop where the technology is concerned.

No doubt Isaacman supports that concept of space-based data centers both because he is astute enough to judge the politics of ground-based versions and because it meshes with his vision of a NASA-led expansion of human civilization beyond Earth. A lunar base devoted to science and exploration is one thing, A lunar settlement that includes mining and manufacturing is quite another. Support for the former may be tenuous and fickle. Support for the latter will be based on real-world economic benefit.

AI will certainly be of benefit for space exploration. The technology will automate spacecraft navigation, speed data analysis and improve astronaut safety through real-time monitoring of systems and predicting failures before they happen.

AI will not replace all human beings on the high frontier of space. AI systems and humans working together will be an unstoppable force that will spread civilization to the moon, Mars and beyond.

Mark R. Whittington, who writes frequently about space policy, has published a political study of space exploration entitled “Why is It So Hard to Go Back to the Moon?” as well as “The Moon, Mars and Beyond” and, most recently, “Why is America Going Back to the Moon?” He blogs at Curmudgeons Corner.

data.title: Trump envoys set for Zelensky meeting after Russia-Ukraine peace talks with Putin
data.description:
President Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff on Sunday made their way to Kyiv to discuss the Ukraine war with the country’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky.

The New York Times reported that Witkoff and Kushner made it to the Ukrainian capital by train and later traveled via motorcade to meet Zelensky. Both CNN and the Times reported that their arrival followed discussion with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.

Witkoff and Kushner were set to travel to Russia and Ukraine this weekend, per previous reports, in an attempt to relaunch peace talks between the two countries. The war between Russia and Ukraine will reach the four-year mark next February if it does not conclude before then.

Zelensky said that he and his own negotiating team had met prior to discussions with Witkoff and Kushner, according to CNN.

“We are ready for talks. Ukraine has always been and will continue to be constructive,” Zelensky said on Telegram, per CNN.

Zelensky posted a video of himself hugging both Witkoff and Kushner on the social platform X Sunday morning. The Ukrainian leader said that the two sides “began talks,” in the caption.

Last Tuesday, Zelensky advised airlines against entering Russian airspace as his military responded to an “escalation” in missile and drone attacks.

The Ukrainian president said in an address that Russia had recently switched up its defense tactics, turning toward strikes from Ukrainian airspace. In the wake of a wave of attacks, Zelensky said that type of warfare “cannot and will not remain confined” to his country’s territory.

data.title: Live updates: Energy secretary set for Sunday show interviews as US, Iran trade strikes
data.description:
Energy Secretary Chris Wright is appearing on four Sunday morning news programs after the U.S. and Iran traded tit-for-tat strikes this weekend.

Iranian officials on Sunday took credit for an attack on an unmanned U.S. military ship in the Strait of Hormuz. That strike came after the U.S. hit three Iranian crude oil carriers in response to “multiple unprovoked” attacks by Iran on two U.S. Navy warships.

Oil prices jumped earlier this week amid earlier renewed strikes by the two countries. The price of Brent crude oil, the international benchmark, hit $96.28 per barrel on Friday.

Wright is also making appearances as controversy swirls around the Trump administration’s Venezuela oil deal. Hill Insiders can read more here.

Elsewhere, the GOP is gearing up for the Republican National Committee’s first-of-its-kind midterm convention in Texas this week, but some are already looking two years ahead. Here’s where the potential Republican 2028 presidential election contenders stand.

President Trump is at his golf club in Bedminster, N.J., with no public events scheduled as of Sunday morning.

Follow live below.

data.title: Iran attacks US ship in Strait of Hormuz
data.description:
Iran has said that it attacked an American ship in the Strait of Hormuz, according to state media.

Iranian state-run media outlet Press TV reported Sunday that a U.S. military vessel, which was remotely-operated, had been attacked by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), according to the military group itself.

Per an IRGC statement, the vessel had been trying to go into a restricted portion in the Strait of Hormuz, Press TV reported.

“With the grace and favor of Almighty God, every desperate move by the enemy is being closely monitored by brave, self-sacrificing IRGC Navy forces and will be met with a decisive attack,” the IRGC said in its Sunday statement, per Press TV.

On Saturday, U.S. Central Command (Centcom) conducted strikes on multiple Iranian crude oil carriers due to “multiple unprovoked” attacks from Iran on two American warships, per the military command.

U.S. forces “permanently disabled” three IRGC crude oil carriers near Kharg Island and in the Gulf of Oman. There were no U.S. service members harmed in the Iranian attacks, Centcom said.

“Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost —taking out three of yours,” Centcom Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said in a statement shared on social media. “We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet.”

Both the U.S. and Iran ramped up their military operations last week. On Tuesday, the U.S. carried out about 100 strikes against Iranian targets, and Tehran responded, targeting U.S. military bases and allies via strikes across the Middle East.

data.title: Trump is waging a war on America's children — and he's winning
data.description:
President Trump’s administration is waging war against children, especially those in our nation’s poorest families. Here are a few of the fronts on which that undeclared war is being fought, with devastating consequences for the next generation of Americans. 

Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act made massive cuts to Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program or SNAP, leaving millions of children in low-income families without access to health insurance, adequate and healthy food and, in some cases, learning and developmental services in public schools.  

Roughly 40 percent of American children receive health coverage through Medicaid. Although the bill’s work requirements do not apply to children, they lose coverage when their parents do. The Congressional Budget Office estimates the cuts will increase the number of Americans without health insurance by 7.5 million in 2034.

The budget office also projects that SNAP spending will decline by $211 billion through 2035. An analysis by the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities estimates 1.5 million children, conservatively, have lost benefits since July 2025. Further reductions are likely as states are forced to pay a larger share of the program’s administrative costs.  

The 2025 bill did increase the Child Tax Credit from $2,000 to $2,200. But it left intact rules that prevent many low-income families from receiving the full credit. As a result, 30 percent of all children and 99 percent of those from the poorest one-fifth of families won’t benefit from the increase.

Each of these individual policies is onerous, but the collective impact is especially damaging, since many families will be hurt by all of them.

The Trump administration’s vaccine policies have put children at risk as well. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and his handpicked appointees have promoted vaccine skepticism, parental choice and limits to state requirements that children be vaccinated before they start school. They claim, without evidence, that COVID-19 vaccines have killed children and that vaccines cause autism.

As a result, vaccination rates are falling. The share of kindergartners exempted from one or more required vaccines has increased from 2.2 percent in 2020-2021 to 4.2 percent in 2025. Only 92 percent of kindergarten students now get the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, well below the 95 percent needed for herd immunity. 

The consequences are not hypothetical. Americans have experienced the largest measles outbreak in three decades, with the vast majority of cases among unvaccinated children. 

Yet Trump’s Aug. 10 executive order pares back the number of recommended childhood vaccines and calls for splitting the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three separately administered shots — changes strongly opposed by mainstream medical organizations because they will leave many more children vulnerable to preventable diseases. 

That same month, the Trump administration proposed deregulating Head Start, one of the country’s most important programs for poor children. Head Start provides preschool, child care, meals and support services to about 700,000 children, many of them homeless, in foster care or disabled. The administration has already closed half of Head Start’s regional offices. Now it intends to reduce the federal overhead payments from 15 percent to 5 percent and eliminate or dilute national standards governing student-teacher ratios, educational requirements, medical screenings, program hours and other services.

The administration claims these changes will reduce costs and allow Head Start to serve more children. But this approach removes requirements intended to bolster program quality. Project 2025, it is worth noting, advocated eliminating Head Start. The administration’s approach will, at a minimum, dramatically reduce its effectiveness.

Meanwhile, tens of thousands of children whose parents have been arrested, detained or deported, or fear they will be, are suffering serious and lasting effects. Faced with economic instability, loss of housing, absence from school, fewer doctor visits, and sometimes foster care, they experience separation anxiety, headaches, stomach aches, difficulty sleeping and eating, and anxiety and depression.

More than 12,000 children and their parents or sponsors have been arrested following tips from the federal Office of Refugee Resettlement, an office that previously maintained a sharp separation between child-welfare responsibilities and immigration enforcement so parents would not be prevented from reuniting with their children. 

Trump’s war on children doesn’t stop at America’s borders. Researchers estimate that reductions in health care, nutrition, clean water and sanitation caused by the evisceration of USAID will lead to the deaths of about 4.5 million children under the age of five by 2030. 

The administration insists its policies will reduce wasteful spending, encourage work, promote parental rights, enforce immigration laws and return authority to the states. But wars are — and should be — measured by their casualties. Across an extraordinary range of administration policies, children, who are least able to protect themselves, are “collateral damage.” 

“Children are the world’s most valuable resource,” President John F. Kennedy proclaimed, “and its best hope for the future.” Apparently, the Trump administration does not agree. 

David Wippman is emeritus president of Hamilton College. Glenn C. Altschuler is the Thomas and Dorothy Litwin Emeritus Professor of American Studies at Cornell University.
